claim: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder in the United States and affects ~1% of the population over the age of 65.
source: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder in the United States and affects ~1% of the population over the age of 65.
evidence: This is a general epidemiological statement about PD prevalence, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: The incidence rate of PD is projected to double between 2015 and 2040, mainly due to lifestyle factors and increased lifespan.
source: The incidence rate of PD is projected to double between 2015 and 2040, mainly due to lifestyle factors and increased lifespan (Dorsey et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dorsey et al., 2018.

claim: Clinical features of PD include slowed movement, muscle rigidity, resting tremors, and postural instability.
source: Clinical features of PD include slowed movement, muscle rigidity, resting tremors, and postural instability.
evidence: This describes well-established clinical symptoms of PD, representing consensus medical knowledge.

claim: PD symptoms result from death of dopaminergic neurons of the nigrostriatal pathway regulating motor function.
source: These symptoms result from death of dopaminergic neurons of the nigrostriatal pathway regulating motor function (Poewe et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Poewe et al., 2017.

claim: Abnormal aggregation of α-synuclein promotes disruptions in multiple cellular processes including mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, proteasomal impairment, autophagy deficits, and neuroinflammation.
source: Abnormal aggregation of the neuronal protein α-synuclein (αSyn) promotes disruptions in multiple cellular processes that contribute to neurodegeneration, including mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, proteasomal impairment, autophagy deficits, and neuroinflammation (Poewe et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Poewe et al., 2017.

claim: 70–80% of PD patients experience gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms, mainly constipation but also abdominal pain and increased intestinal permeability.
source: Although PD is predominantly classified as a brain disorder, 70–80% of patients experience gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms, mainly constipation but also abdominal pain and increased intestinal permeability that usually manifests in the prodromal stages (Forsyth et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Forsyth et al., 2011 and Yang et al., 2019.

claim: Braak's hypothesis postulated that αSyn aggregation may start at peripheral environmental interfaces and eventually reach the brain via the vagus nerve.
source: Braak's hypothesis postulated nearly 20 years ago that αSyn aggregation may start at peripheral environmental interfaces, like the GI tract or olfactory bulb, and eventually reach the brain stem, substantia nigra, and neocortex via the vagus nerve (Braak et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Braak et al., 2003.

claim: Evidence has corroborated the potential for gut-to-brain spread of αSyn pathology in rodents.
source: Increasing evidence has corroborated the potential for gut-to-brain spread of αSyn pathology in rodents (Kim et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2017a; Svensson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2017a; and Svensson et al., 2015.

claim: Several studies have detected differences in gut microbiome composition between PD patients and healthy controls.
source: Additionally, several studies have detected differences in gut microbiome composition between PD patients and healthy controls (Çamcı and Oğuz, 2016; Keshavarzian et al., 2015; Scheperjans et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2014), with decreased abundance of health-promoting bacteria and an increase in pro-inflammatory pathogenic bacteria in the PD microbiome.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Çamcı and Oğuz, 2016; Keshavarzian et al., 2015; Scheperjans et al., 2015; and Tan et al., 2014.

claim: The PD microbiome shows decreased abundance of health-promoting bacteria and an increase in pro-inflammatory pathogenic bacteria.
source: Additionally, several studies have detected differences in gut microbiome composition between PD patients and healthy controls (Çamcı and Oğuz, 2016; Keshavarzian et al., 2015; Scheperjans et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2014), with decreased abundance of health-promoting bacteria and an increase in pro-inflammatory pathogenic bacteria in the PD microbiome.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on PD microbiome composition.

claim: Altering the microbiome in α-synuclein overexpressing (ASO) mice modulates brain pathology and motor performance.
source: Altering the microbiome in α-synuclein overexpressing (ASO) mice modulates brain pathology and motor performance (Sampson et al., 2016), and gut bacterial species have been shown to accelerate disease in other PD mouse models (Choi et al., 2018; Sampson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sampson et al., 2016.

claim: Gut bacterial species have been shown to accelerate disease in PD mouse models.
source: Altering the microbiome in α-synuclein overexpressing (ASO) mice modulates brain pathology and motor performance (Sampson et al., 2016), and gut bacterial species have been shown to accelerate disease in other PD mouse models (Choi et al., 2018; Sampson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2018 and Sampson et al., 2020.

claim: Antibiotic treatment improves motor symptoms in several models of PD.
source: Additionally, antibiotic treatment improves motor symptoms in several models of PD (Cui et al., 2022; Pu et al., 2019; Sampson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cui et al., 2022; Pu et al., 2019; and Sampson et al., 2016.

claim: Microglia can shape neural circuity through regulation of neurogenesis, synaptic pruning, and myelination.
source: One potential target of gut-brain signaling in PD are microglia, a versatile macrophage-like population of brain cells that can shape neural circuity through regulation of neurogenesis, synaptic pruning, and myelination (Anderson and Vetter, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anderson and Vetter, 2019.

claim: In PD and other neurodegenerative conditions, microglial cellular repair responses become dysregulated, resulting in heightened reactivity and chronic inflammation that drives neurodegeneration.
source: In PD and other neurodegenerative conditions, microglial cellular repair responses are thought to become dysregulated, ultimately resulting in heightened reactivity and chronic inflammation that drives neurodegeneration (Troncoso-Escudero et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Troncoso-Escudero et al., 2018.

claim: Microglia respond to signals from the periphery including from the gut microbiome.
source: Microglia respond to signals from within the brain, but also receive input from the periphery including from the gut microbiome (Abdel-Haq et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Abdel-Haq et al., 2019.

claim: Offspring of germ-free (GF) mice show differences in microglial gene expression and chromatin accessibility compared to specific-pathogen-free (SPF) counterparts.
source: Offspring of germ-free (GF) mice show differences in microglial gene expression and chromatin accessibility compared to specific-pathogen-free (SPF) counterparts (Thion et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thion et al., 2018.

claim: Microglia from adult GF mice present an immature gene expression profile and fail to adequately respond to immunostimulants.
source: Microglia from adult GF mice present an immature gene expression profile and fail to adequately respond to immunostimulants (Erny et al., 2015; Thion et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Erny et al., 2015 and Thion et al., 2018.

claim: Feeding GF mice a mixture of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) is sufficient to rescue microglial maturation.
source: However, feeding GF mice a mixture of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), metabolic products of bacterial fiber fermentation, is sufficient to rescue microglial maturation (Erny et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Erny et al., 2015.

claim: Levels of SCFAs are reduced in fecal samples from PD patients compared to matched controls.
source: Interestingly, levels of SCFAs are reduced in fecal samples from PD patients compared to matched controls (Chen et al., 2022; Unger et al., 2016) and inversely correlate with disease severity (Aho et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2022 and Unger et al., 2016.

claim: SCFA levels inversely correlate with PD disease severity.
source: Interestingly, levels of SCFAs are reduced in fecal samples from PD patients compared to matched controls (Chen et al., 2022; Unger et al., 2016) and inversely correlate with disease severity (Aho et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aho et al., 2021 and Chen et al., 2022.

claim: The ASO mouse model recapitulates many hallmark symptoms of PD including motor deficits, GI abnormalities, olfactory dysfunction, and neuroinflammation.
source: Herein, we explore the interplay between diet and microglia in the ASO mouse model, which recapitulates many of the hallmark symptoms of PD including motor deficits, GI abnormalities, olfactory dysfunction, and neuroinflammation (Chesselet et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chesselet et al., 2012.

claim: A prebiotic diet remodels the gut microbiome of ASO mice to contain increased relative abundances of taxa linked to outcomes associated with health.
source: We demonstrate that a prebiotic diet remodels the gut microbiome of ASO mice to contain increased relative abundances of taxa linked to outcomes associated with health.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from metagenomic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Prebiotic intervention attenuates motor deficits in ASO mice.
source: Prebiotic intervention attenuates motor deficits and reduces αSyn aggregates in the substantia nigra of ASO mice in a microglia-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by motor behavior test data presented in Figure 1A-D.

claim: Prebiotic intervention reduces αSyn aggregates in the substantia nigra of ASO mice.
source: Prebiotic intervention attenuates motor deficits and reduces αSyn aggregates in the substantia nigra of ASO mice in a microglia-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by dot blot data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: The beneficial effects of prebiotic intervention in ASO mice are microglia-dependent.
source: Prebiotic intervention attenuates motor deficits and reduces αSyn aggregates in the substantia nigra of ASO mice in a microglia-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by microglial depletion experiments using PLX5622 presented in Figure 5.

claim: Prebiotic diet alters the morphology and gene expression patterns of microglia in brain regions involved in PD.
source: Prebiotic diet alters the morphology and gene expression patterns of microglia in brain regions involved in PD, promoting phenotypes associated with disease-protective responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data (Figure 3) and scRNA-seq data (Figure 4).

claim: Microglial depletion abrogates the beneficial effects of prebiotics in ASO mice.
source: Importantly, microglial depletion abrogates the beneficial effects of prebiotics.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from PLX5622 treatment experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Enhanced metabolism of dietary fiber by the gut microbiome alters the physiology of cells in the CNS and improves behavioral and pathologic outcomes in ASO mice.
source: Overall, this study reveals that enhanced metabolism of dietary fiber by the gut microbiome alters the physiology of cells in the CNS and ultimately improves behavioral and pathologic outcomes in a mouse model of PD.
evidence: This is a summary claim integrating multiple experimental findings from the study.

claim: Three custom high-fiber diets were generated, each containing 20% of a prebiotic mixture of two or three dietary fibers.
source: We generated three custom high-fiber diets (Supplementary file 1), each containing 20% of a prebiotic mixture of two or three dietary fibers designed to promote growth of distinct gut bacterial taxa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and boost SCFA production (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-E) based on in vitro fecal fermentation.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is supported by data in supplementary figures.

claim: The prebiotic diets were designed to promote growth of distinct gut bacterial taxa and boost SCFA production based on in vitro fecal fermentation.
source: We generated three custom high-fiber diets (Supplementary file 1), each containing 20% of a prebiotic mixture of two or three dietary fibers designed to promote growth of distinct gut bacterial taxa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and boost SCFA production (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-E) based on in vitro fecal fermentation.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro fermentation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Administration of prebiotic diet #1 to ASO mice enhanced performance in pole descent and beam traversal tests compared to mice fed a control diet.
source: Remarkably, administration of the prebiotic diet to ASO mice enhanced performance in several motor behavioral tests, including the pole descent and beam traversal tests (time to cross, steps to cross, errors per step) compared to mice fed a control diet (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by motor behavior data shown in Figure 1A-D.

claim: Outcomes in adhesive removal, wire hang, and hindlimb score tests were unchanged by prebiotic diet.
source: Outcomes in other paradigms including adhesive removal, wire hang, and hindlimb score were unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by motor behavior data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-C.

claim: A gut-targeting intervention has the potential to attenuate key behavioral features in a mouse model of PD.
source: These findings reveal that a gut-targeting intervention has the potential to attenuate key behavioral features in a mouse model of PD.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the motor behavior improvements observed with prebiotic treatment.

claim: Levels of all major SCFAs were higher in fecal samples from prebiotic-fed mice than from control-fed mice.
source: As anticipated, levels of all major SCFAs were higher in fecal samples from prebiotic-fed mice than from control-fed mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by SCFA measurement data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Concentrations of propionate, butyrate, and isobutyrate were not significantly different between wild type (WT) and ASO mice fed a control diet.
source: Concentrations of propionate, butyrate, and isobutyrate were not significantly different between wild type (WT) and ASO mice fed a control diet (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by SCFA measurement data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: ASO mice weighed significantly less than their WT counterparts.
source: ASO mice weighed significantly less than their WT counterparts and exhibited reduced food intake of control diet, but not prebiotic diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D-E).
evidence: This claim is supported by weight and food intake data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D-E.

claim: ASO mice exhibited reduced food intake of control diet, but not prebiotic diet.
source: ASO mice weighed significantly less than their WT counterparts and exhibited reduced food intake of control diet, but not prebiotic diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D-E).
evidence: This claim is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Prebiotic-ASO mice ate significantly more than control-ASO mice.
source: While prebiotic-ASO mice ate significantly more than control-ASO mice, no difference in body weight was detected between the groups at 22 weeks of age (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

claim: No difference in body weight was detected between prebiotic-ASO and control-ASO mice at 22 weeks of age.
source: While prebiotic-ASO mice ate significantly more than control-ASO mice, no difference in body weight was detected between the groups at 22 weeks of age (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by weight data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Prebiotic feeding significantly reduced αSyn aggregation in the substantia nigra of ASO mice compared to control diet.
source: We found a significant reduction in αSyn aggregation in the substantia nigra (SN) of prebiotic-fed ASO mice compared to ASO mice on control chow (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by dot blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Prebiotic intervention had no effect on αSyn aggregation in the striatum.
source: In contrast, prebiotic intervention had no effect on αSyn aggregation in the striatum (STR) (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by dot blot data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Regional differences in microglia density, gene expression, and clearance activity may explain differential effects of prebiotics on αSyn aggregation in SN versus striatum.
source: We speculate that this difference may be attributable to regional differences in microglia density, gene expression, and clearance activity (Grabert et al., 2016; Y.-L. Tan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Grabert et al., 2016 and Y.-L. Tan et al., 2020.

claim: Early intervention with a prebiotic diet can reduce PD-like symptoms and brain pathology in ASO mice.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that early intervention with a prebiotic diet can reduce PD-like symptoms and brain pathology in ASO mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the motor behavior and αSyn aggregation data.

claim: Alpha diversity analysis revealed significant reduction in observed species count, Shannon's diversity, and Simpson's evenness in prebiotic-fed groups.
source: Alpha diversity analysis revealed significant reduction in observed species count, Shannon's diversity, and Simpson's evenness in prebiotic-fed groups, as well as an increase in Gini's dominance (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by metagenomic diversity analysis data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: Prebiotic-fed groups showed an increase in Gini's dominance.
source: Alpha diversity analysis revealed significant reduction in observed species count, Shannon's diversity, and Simpson's evenness in prebiotic-fed groups, as well as an increase in Gini's dominance (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by metagenomic diversity analysis data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Reduced microbiome diversity in high-fiber fed mice is consistent with a previous report.
source: This is consistent with a previous report of reduced microbiome diversity in high-fiber fed mice (Luo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Luo et al., 2017.

claim: Fecal samples clustered more closely by diet than mouse genotype in principal coordinate analysis.
source: Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) of species abundance showed that samples clustered more closely by diet than mouse genotype (Figure 2E) and PERMANOVA revealed that prebiotic treatment explained 6-fold more variance than genotype, with R2 values of 0.334 and 0.053 for each, respectively (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCoA and PERMANOVA analysis shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Prebiotic treatment explained 6-fold more variance than genotype in microbiome composition (R2 values of 0.334 vs 0.053).
source: Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) of species abundance showed that samples clustered more closely by diet than mouse genotype (Figure 2E) and PERMANOVA revealed that prebiotic treatment explained 6-fold more variance than genotype, with R2 values of 0.334 and 0.053 for each, respectively (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by PERMANOVA analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The prebiotic diet reshapes gut microbial communities in WT and ASO mice.
source: Thus, the prebiotic diet reshapes gut microbial communities in WT and ASO mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the metagenomic analysis data.

claim: Prebiotic diet feeding resulted in an increase in Bacteroidetes and a decrease in Firmicutes, resulting in a lower Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes (F/B) ratio.
source: We observed broad changes at the microbial phylum and genus levels following administration of prebiotic diet (Figure 2G and I), displaying an increase in Bacteroidetes and a decrease in Firmicutes in prebiotic diet-fed mice, resulting in a lower Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes (F/B) ratio that has been associated with general features of metabolic health (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by metagenomic data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: A lower Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio has been associated with general features of metabolic health.
source: We observed broad changes at the microbial phylum and genus levels following administration of prebiotic diet (Figure 2G and I), displaying an increase in Bacteroidetes and a decrease in Firmicutes in prebiotic diet-fed mice, resulting in a lower Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes (F/B) ratio that has been associated with general features of metabolic health (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the F/B ratio and metabolic health.

claim: Bacteroidetes are reduced in PD patients compared to age-matched controls.
source: Intriguingly, it has been shown that Bacteroidetes are reduced in PD patients compared to age-matched controls, suggesting the prebiotic may counter this effect (Unger et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Unger et al., 2016.

claim: Prebiotic diet resulted in a decrease in Proteobacteria, a phylum often increased in dysbiosis and inflammation and elevated in PD patient fecal samples.
source: Additionally, we observed a decrease in Proteobacteria, a phylum often increased in dysbiosis and inflammation and elevated in PD patient fecal samples (Figure 2H; Keshavarzian et al., 2015; Shin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by metagenomic data in Figure 2H and citations to Keshavarzian et al., 2015 and Shin et al., 2015.

claim: Gut-brain module analysis showed variation in metabolic pathways including SCFA degradation/synthesis in response to diet and genotype.
source: Gut-brain module analysis showed variation in metabolic pathways including SCFA degradation/synthesis in response to diet and genotype (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by gut-brain module analysis data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Feeding of a prebiotic diet restructures the ASO microbiome toward increased relative abundances of taxa associated with potentially protective effects.
source: Overall, feeding of a prebiotic diet appears to qualitatively restructure the ASO microbiome toward increased relative abundances of taxa associated with potentially protective effects.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the metagenomic analysis data.

claim: In ASO mice, microglia reactivity in response to αSyn overexpression appears at 4–5 weeks of age in the STR and at 20–24 weeks of age in the SN.
source: In ASO mice, microglia reactivity in response to αSyn overexpression appears at 4–5 weeks of age in the STR and at 20–24 weeks of age in the SN (Watson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Watson et al., 2012.

claim: SCFAs have been shown to influence the physiology of microglia in several contexts.
source: SCFAs have been shown to influence the physiology of microglia in several contexts (Colombo et al., 2021; Erny et al., 2015; Sadler et al., 2020; Erny et al., 2021; Sampson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Homeostatic microglia exhibit a ramified shape with a smaller cell body and increased dendritic processes.
source: The morphology of microglia can indicate their reactivity state, with homeostatic microglia exhibiting a ramified shape with a smaller cell body and increased dendritic processes, whereas activated microglia adopt an amoeboid form with a larger cell body and retracted processes (Menassa and Gomez-Nicola, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Menassa and Gomez-Nicola, 2018.

claim: Activated microglia adopt an amoeboid form with a larger cell body and retracted processes.
source: The morphology of microglia can indicate their reactivity state, with homeostatic microglia exhibiting a ramified shape with a smaller cell body and increased dendritic processes, whereas activated microglia adopt an amoeboid form with a larger cell body and retracted processes (Menassa and Gomez-Nicola, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Menassa and Gomez-Nicola, 2018.

claim: Microglia in the SN and STR of prebiotic-ASO mice had significantly smaller cell bodies than in control-ASO mice.
source: We observed that microglia in the SN and STR of prebiotic-ASO mice had significantly smaller cell bodies than in control-ASO mice (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by IBA1 immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Microglia in the SN and STR of prebiotic-ASO mice exhibited increased dendrite length, number of segments, number of branch points, and number of terminal points compared to control-ASO mice.
source: 3D analysis of key morphological features revealed that microglia in the SN and STR of prebiotic-ASO mice exhibited increased dendrite length, number of segments, number of branch points, and number of terminal points compared to microglia from control-ASO mice (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D reconstruction analysis data shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: Long-term prebiotic intervention dampens microglial reactivity in brain regions implicated in PD.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that long-term prebiotic intervention dampens microglial reactivity in brain regions implicated in PD.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the microglial morphology data.

claim: Differential gene expression analysis revealed 313 differentially expressed genes (163 upregulated, 150 downregulated) in the SN between control-WT and control-ASO mice.
source: Differential gene expression analysis of all cells revealed 313 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (↑163, ↓150, FDR <0.05) in the SN and 997 DEGs (↑511, ↓486) in the STR.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: Differential gene expression analysis revealed 997 differentially expressed genes (511 upregulated, 486 downregulated) in the STR between control-WT and control-ASO mice.
source: Differential gene expression analysis of all cells revealed 313 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (↑163, ↓150, FDR <0.05) in the SN and 997 DEGs (↑511, ↓486) in the STR.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: In the SN, microglia from control-ASO mice displayed increased expression of MHC class I components, several chemokines and chemokine receptors, and pro-inflammatory markers.
source: In the SN, microglia harvested from control-ASO mice displayed increased expression of MHC class I components (H2-K1, H2-D1), several chemokines (Ccl2, Ccl3, Ccl4, Ccl9) and chemokine receptors (Ccr1, Ccr5), and pro-inflammatory markers (Nfkbid, Cd 74) (Figure 4C, Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4C and Supplementary file 2a.

claim: Gene enrichment analysis of upregulated DEGs in control-ASO mice showed enrichment in pathways related to cellular responses to cytokine stimulus and interferon-gamma, immune system processes, and response to stress.
source: Gene enrichment analysis of all upregulated DEGs in control-ASO mice showed enrichment in pathways related to cellular responses to cytokine stimulus and interferon-gamma, immune system processes, and response to stress (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Several genes downregulated in control-ASO mice compared to control-WT were related to anti-inflammatory signaling and microglial homeostasis.
source: Several genes that were downregulated in control-ASO mice compared to control-WT were related to anti-inflammatory signaling (Klf2, Klf4) and microglial homeostasis (P2ry12, Slc2a5) (Figure 4C, Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4C and Supplementary file 2a.

claim: Control-ASO microglia in the STR upregulated pro-inflammatory modulators and antigen processing and presentation genes.
source: We observed similar trends in the STR, with control-ASO microglia upregulating pro-inflammatory modulators (Tnf, Nfkbiz, Trim8, Irgm1) and antigen processing and presentation genes (H2-Q7, H2-K1, H2-D1, H2-T23) and downregulating genes related to homeostatic cellular processes (Figure 4H–I, Supplementary file 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4H-I and Supplementary file 2c.

claim: The anti-inflammatory cytokine transforming growth factor beta 2 (Tgfβ2) was ~45-fold downregulated in control-ASO microglia in the STR.
source: Notably, the anti-inflammatory cytokine transforming growth factor beta 2 (Tgfβ2) was ~45-fold downregulated in control-ASO (Supplementary file 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data in Supplementary file 2c.

claim: Microglia from control-ASO mice upregulate pro-inflammatory immune processes and downregulate pathways related to homeostasis and cellular maintenance in response to αSyn overexpression.
source: These data suggest microglia from control-ASO mice upregulate pro-inflammatory immune processes and downregulate pathways related to homeostasis and cellular maintenance in response to αSyn overexpression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the scRNA-seq differential expression data.

claim: UMAP analysis yielded nine distinct microglia clusters in the SN and eight clusters in the STR based on global scRNA-seq gene expression.
source: Based on global scRNA-seq gene expression, Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction (UMAP) analysis yielded nine distinct microglia clusters in the SN and eight clusters in the STR (Figure 4A and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by UMAP analysis shown in Figure 4A and F.

claim: The percentage of microglia in cluster 0 was higher in control-ASO than control-WT mice (27.1% vs 18.9%), and prebiotic treatment reduced this to 18.3%.
source: Interestingly, the percentage of microglia in cluster 0 was higher in control-ASO than control-WT mice (27.1% vs 18.9%), and prebiotic treatment reduced the percentage of microglia belonging to cluster 0 in ASO mice compared to control diets (18.3%) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster distribution data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Gene enrichment analysis of cluster 0 revealed pathways related to immune system processes, cellular response to TNF, cellular response to lipopolysaccharide, and response to stress.
source: Gene enrichment analysis of the top 50 genes associated with cluster 0 revealed pathways related to immune system processes, cellular response to tumor necrosis factor (TNF), cellular response to lipopolysaccharide, and response to stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene enrichment analysis of cluster 0.

claim: Cluster 0 contained several prominent immune markers including Tnf, Nfkbia, Ccl2, Ccl3, and Ccl4.
source: Cluster 0 contained several prominent immune markers including Tnf, Nfkbia, Ccl2, Ccl3, and Ccl4, suggesting that a prebiotic diet may suppress or prevent pro-inflammatory responses in ASO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq cluster analysis data.

claim: Levels of TNF and Ccl2 are elevated in the serum of PD patients.
source: Notably, levels of TNF and Ccl2 are elevated in the serum of PD patients (Brodacki et al., 2008; Reale et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brodacki et al., 2008 and Reale et al., 2009.

claim: The percentage of microglia belonging to cluster 2 was reduced in control-ASO mice but increased in prebiotic-ASO mice.
source: Conversely, the percentage of microglia belonging to cluster 2 was reduced in control-ASO mice but increased in prebiotic-ASO mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster distribution data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Among the most highly expressed genes in cluster 2 were the homeostatic microglial markers P2ry12 and Cst3, as well as the anti-inflammatory transcription factors Klf2 and Klf4.
source: Among the most highly expressed genes in cluster 2 were the homeostatic microglial markers P2ry12 and Cst3, as well as the anti-inflammatory transcription factors Klf2 and Klf4 (Das et al., 2006; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq cluster analysis data and citations to Das et al., 2006 and Li et al., 2018.

claim: The top 10 associative genes in cluster 3 in the STR included several mitochondrial genes.
source: The top 10 associative genes in cluster 3 included several mitochondrial genes: mt-Atp6, mt-Cytb, mt-Co2, mt-Co3, mt-Nd4, mt-Nd1, and mt-Nd2.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq cluster analysis data.

claim: A 13.4% increase in cluster 1 was detected in control-ASO mice, with prebiotic diet restoring the percentage back to control-WT levels.
source: Additionally, we detected a 13.4% increase in cluster 1 in control-ASO mice, with prebiotic diet restoring the percentage of cluster 1 back to control-WT levels (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster distribution data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Significantly enriched pathways within cluster 1 included those positively regulating cell death and immune system development, and negatively regulating cellular processes.
source: The significantly enriched pathways within cluster 1 included those positively regulating cell death and immune system development, and negatively regulating cellular processes, suggesting increased immune signaling and dysregulation of homeostatic signaling in the absence of prebiotic treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene enrichment analysis of cluster 1.

claim: Comparison of prebiotic-ASO to control-ASO microglia found 473 DEGs (317 upregulated, 156 downregulated) in the SN and 1474 DEGs (608 upregulated, 866 downregulated) in the STR.
source: To determine effects of long-term prebiotic exposure on microglial gene expression in ASO mice, we compared prebiotic-ASO microglia to control-ASO and found 473 DEGs (↑317, ↓156) in the SN and 1474 DEGs (↑608, ↓866) in the STR (Figure 4C and H, Supplementary file 2b, d).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: Gene enrichment analysis of the 156 genes downregulated in prebiotic-ASO microglia in the SN revealed reduction in IL-1β production pathways, innate immune response, and defense response pathways.
source: Gene enrichment analysis of the 156 genes downregulated in prebiotic-ASO microglia in the SN revealed reduction in interleukin-1 (IL-1)β production pathways, as well as dampened innate immune response and defense response pathways compared to control-ASO mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Among the genes downregulated in microglia from prebiotic-ASO mice were several mediators of pro-inflammatory immune response, antigen presentation and processing, and chemokines/receptors.
source: Among the genes downregulated in microglia from prebiotic-ASO mice were several mediators of the pro-inflammatory immune response (Mif, Masp1, Trim12a, Bs2, B2m), antigen presentation and processing (H2-Q7), and chemokines/receptors (Ccl9, Ccr1, Ccr5) (Figure 4C, Supplementary file 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4C and Supplementary file 2b.

claim: In the STR, prebiotic-ASO showed downregulation of pathways related to innate immunity, response to stress, and defense response.
source: We observed a similar trend in the STR, with prebiotic-ASO showing downregulation of pathways related to innate immunity, response to stress, and defense response (Figure 4H and J, Supplementary file 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 4H and J.

claim: Several pro-inflammatory markers upregulated in control-ASO and downregulated in prebiotic-ASO microglia were expressed by a small subset of microglia.
source: Interestingly, several of the pro-inflammatory markers upregulated in control-ASO and downregulated in prebiotic-ASO microglia were expressed by a small subset of microglia, suggesting that a subpopulation of cells alters its transcriptomic profile in response to αSyn expression, similar to what has been observed in microglia from aged mice and a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Hammond et al., 2019; Keren-Shaul et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data and citations to Hammond et al., 2019 and Keren-Shaul et al., 2017.

claim: DEG analysis revealed increased expression of several markers that define disease-associated macrophages (DAM) in the SN and STR in prebiotic-ASO mice.
source: Further DEG analysis revealed increased expression of several markers that define disease-associated macrophages (DAM) in the SN and STR in prebiotic-ASO mice (Supplementary file 2b, d), a microglial sub-population associated with protection during early stages of disease in several mouse models (Deczkowska et al., 2018; Onuska, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data in Supplementary file 2b, d and citations to Deczkowska et al., 2018 and Onuska, 2020.

claim: DAM is a microglial sub-population associated with protection during early stages of disease in several mouse models.
source: Further DEG analysis revealed increased expression of several markers that define disease-associated macrophages (DAM) in the SN and STR in prebiotic-ASO mice (Supplementary file 2b, d), a microglial sub-population associated with protection during early stages of disease in several mouse models (Deczkowska et al., 2018; Onuska, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deczkowska et al., 2018 and Onuska, 2020.

claim: An increase in Trem2 was observed in microglia from the STR of prebiotic-ASO mice.
source: Notably, we observed an increase in Trem2 in microglia from the STR of prebiotic-ASO mice, suggesting prebiotics may induce a neuroprotective DAM phenotype by 22 weeks of age (Gratuze et al., 2018; Keren-Shaul et al., 2017; Onuska, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data and citations to Gratuze et al., 2018; Keren-Shaul et al., 2017; and Onuska, 2020.

claim: Prebiotic intervention in ASO mice dampens proinflammatory and neurotoxic signaling pathways and potentially upregulates a neuroprotective phenotype in microglia.
source: Taken together, gene expression analysis suggests prebiotic intervention in ASO mice dampens proinflammatory and neurotoxic signaling pathways and potentially upregulates a neuroprotective phenotype in microglia.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the scRNA-seq gene expression analysis.

claim: No differences in SCFA levels were detected between control and prebiotic animal groups in either the SN or STR.
source: We detected no differences in SCFA levels between control and prebiotic animal groups in either the SN or STR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SCFA measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: SCFAs can signal through activation of GPCR receptors (FFAR2 and FFAR3) and/or inhibition of histone deacetylases (HDACs).
source: SCFAs can signal through activation of GPCR receptors (GPCR43 or FFAR2, and GPCR41 or FFAR3) and/or inhibition of histone deacetylases (HDACs), altering the epigenetic landscape of target cells (Silva et al., 2020; Vinolo et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Silva et al., 2020 and Vinolo et al., 2011.

claim: ASO mice exhibited very low or no expression of FFAR2 and FFAR3 in the cerebellum, midbrain, striatum, and motor cortex relative to the small intestine.
source: As determined via qRT-PCR, ASO mice exhibited very low or no expression of FFAR2 and FFAR3 in the cerebellum, midbrain, striatum, and motor cortex relative to the small intestine (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B), consistent with scRNA-seq data showing an absence of FFAR2/3 expression in microglia in the SN and STR (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B and scRNA-seq data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Bulk ATAC-seq on purified microglia from the SN and STR showed no significant differences in chromatin accessibility between experimental groups.
source: To explore whether the prebiotic diet was inducing epigenetic changes, we performed bulk ATAC-seq on purified microglia from the SN and STR and observed no significant differences in chromatin accessibility between experimental groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: No differences in expression levels of several HDAC isoforms (Hdac 1, 2, 6, 7, and 9) were found in the striatum between control and prebiotic groups.
source: We also measured the expression levels of several HDAC isoforms (Hdac 1, 2, 6, 7, and 9) in the striatum and found no differences in expression between control and prebiotic groups of both genotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E-I).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E-I.

claim: Dietary metabolites may influence microglial gene expression through indirect mechanisms and likely not by entering the brain.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that dietary metabolites may influence microglial gene expression through indirect mechanisms and likely not by entering the brain, consistent with previous reports (Erny et al., 2015), though additional work is needed to validate this hypothesis.
evidence: This is speculation based on the SCFA, FFAR, ATAC-seq, and HDAC data, supported by a citation to Erny et al., 2015.

claim: PLX5622 is a brain-penetrant inhibitor of CSF1R that can deplete microglia with no observed effects on behavior or cognition.
source: PLX5622 is a brain-penetrant inhibitor of CSF1R that can deplete microglia with no observed effects on behavior or cognition (Elmore et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Elmore et al., 2014.

claim: The efficiency of microglial depletion by PLX5622 varied depending on brain region, with the cerebellum showing ~80% depletion, SN ~65%, and STR ~75%.
source: The efficiency of microglial depletion varied depending on brain region, with regions containing low numbers of microglia such as the cerebellum exhibiting higher depletion (~80%) than areas with high microglial density such as the SN (~65%) and STR (~75%) (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by IBA1+ cell count data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: No differences in depletion efficiency were observed between WT and ASO mice or between control and prebiotic-fed mice.
source: We did not observe differences in depletion efficiency between WT and ASO mice or between control and prebiotic-fed mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This claim is supported by IBA1+ cell count data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: PLX5622 treatment had no impact on motor performance in tests where prebiotic treatment had no effect.
source: PLX5622 treatment had no impact on motor performance in tests where prebiotic treatment had no effect (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-F).
evidence: This claim is supported by motor behavior data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: Even incomplete microglia depletion eliminated prebiotic-induced improvements in the pole descent and beam traversal tests.
source: Remarkably however, even incomplete microglia depletion eliminated prebiotic-induced improvements in the pole descent and beam traversal tests (time to cross, errors per step) (Figure 5D–F), suggesting that microglia are required for the ability of prebiotics to ameliorate motor deficits.
evidence: This claim is supported by motor behavior data with PLX5622 treatment shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: Microglia are required for the ability of prebiotics to ameliorate motor deficits in ASO mice.
source: Remarkably however, even incomplete microglia depletion eliminated prebiotic-induced improvements in the pole descent and beam traversal tests (time to cross, errors per step) (Figure 5D–F), suggesting that microglia are required for the ability of prebiotics to ameliorate motor deficits.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PLX5622 motor behavior data.

claim: PLX5622 treatment did not alter body weight in control or prebiotic-fed mice.
source: PLX5622 treatment did not alter body weight in control or prebiotic-fed mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by weight data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: In control-fed mice, depletion of microglia had no impact on levels of αSyn aggregation in the SN or STR.
source: In control-fed mice, depletion of microglia had no impact on levels of αSyn aggregation in the SN or STR (Figure 5G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by dot blot data shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: In prebiotic-fed WT and ASO mice, depletion of microglia significantly increased levels of aggregated αSyn in the SN, while levels in the STR remained unchanged.
source: However, in prebiotic-fed WT and ASO mice, depletion of microglia significantly increased levels of aggregated αSyn in the SN, while levels in the STR remained unchanged (Figure 5G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by dot blot data shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: Partial ablation of microglia or diminished CSF1R signaling eliminate the protective effects of the prebiotic diet in ASO mice.
source: These data reveal that partial ablation of microglia or diminished CSF1R signaling eliminate the protective effects of the prebiotic diet in ASO mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PLX5622 treatment data on motor behavior and αSyn aggregation.

claim: Most gut-associated immune cell populations were unaffected by PLX5622 treatment.
source: Surprisingly, most gut-associated immune cell populations were unaffected by PLX5622 treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the large intestine, PLX5622 treatment caused a reduction in CD45+ CSF1Rlo lymphocytes, but had no impact on CD45+ CSF1Rhi cells, pan T cells or B cells.
source: In the large intestine, PLX5622 treatment caused a reduction in CD45+ CSF1Rlo lymphocytes, but had no impact on CD45+ CSF1Rhi cells, pan T cells or B cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-E.

claim: In the small intestine, levels of immune cell types were unchanged in response to PLX5622.
source: In the small intestine, levels of these cell types were unchanged in response to PLX5622 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F-J).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2F-J.

claim: In the spleen, CSF1Rlo lymphocytes were reduced in Prebiotic +PLX5622 mice, but levels of CSF1Rhi macrophages were significantly elevated in Control +PLX5622 and Prebiotic +PLX5622 mice.
source: In the spleen, while CSF1Rlo lymphocytes were reduced in Prebiotic +PLX5622 mice, levels of CSF1Rhi macrophages were significantly elevated in Control +PLX5622 and Prebiotic +PLX5622 mice, suggesting a potential compensatory mechanism in this organ (Figure 5—figure supplement 2K-O).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2K-O.

claim: The findings point to a relatively high specificity of CSF1R-targeted depletion in the brain, further implicating microglia as a key mediator of the beneficial effects of prebiotic treatment in ASO mice.
source: These findings point to a relatively high specificity of CSF1R-targeted depletion in the brain, further implicating microglia as a key mediator of the beneficial effects of prebiotic treatment in ASO mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PLX5622 immune cell profiling data.

claim: The mechanism by which a high-fiber diet influences microglial physiology and alters behavior remains unclear.
source: The mechanism by which a high-fiber diet influences microglial physiology and alters behavior remains unclear.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the current study.

claim: SCFA levels in the brain tissue of prebiotic-fed mice were unchanged.
source: SCFA levels in the brain tissue of prebiotic-fed mice were unchanged, and our data suggest that SCFAs do not appear to signal through known GPCRs in the brain or via epigenetic remodeling of microglia-derived chromatin, further reinforcing the notion of indirect effects on microglia, as previously suggested (Erny et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by SCFA measurement data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: SCFAs do not appear to signal through known GPCRs in the brain or via epigenetic remodeling of microglia-derived chromatin.
source: SCFA levels in the brain tissue of prebiotic-fed mice were unchanged, and our data suggest that SCFAs do not appear to signal through known GPCRs in the brain or via epigenetic remodeling of microglia-derived chromatin, further reinforcing the notion of indirect effects on microglia, as previously suggested (Erny et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on FFAR expression, ATAC-seq, and HDAC expression data, supported by a citation to Erny et al., 2015.

claim: SCFAs are known to have immune modulatory properties in the gut.
source: SCFAs are known to have immune modulatory properties in the gut (Parada Venegas et al., 2019), among other functions, and we speculate that altering peripheral immunity may affect microglial reactivity states and gene expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Parada Venegas et al., 2019.

claim: Altering peripheral immunity may affect microglial reactivity states and gene expression.
source: SCFAs are known to have immune modulatory properties in the gut (Parada Venegas et al., 2019), among other functions, and we speculate that altering peripheral immunity may affect microglial reactivity states and gene expression.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: It is possible molecules other than SCFAs may be contributing to prebiotic-induced changes in microglial physiology.
source: We note that it is possible molecules other than SCFAs may be contributing to prebiotic-induced changes in microglial physiology, a notion we are unable to test in the ASO mouse model.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of alternative possibilities and study limitations.

claim: Oral administration of SCFAs to GF mice induces microglial reactivity in wild-type mice.
source: Oral administration of SCFAs to GF mice induces microglial reactivity in wild-type mice (Erny et al., 2015), a mouse model of AD (Colombo et al., 2021), and ASO mice, where feeding the metabolites in the absence of gut bacteria exacerbates motor deficits and neuroinflammation (Sampson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Erny et al., 2015, Colombo et al., 2021, and Sampson et al., 2016.

claim: Feeding SCFAs to ASO mice in the absence of gut bacteria exacerbates motor deficits and neuroinflammation.
source: Oral administration of SCFAs to GF mice induces microglial reactivity in wild-type mice (Erny et al., 2015), a mouse model of AD (Colombo et al., 2021), and ASO mice, where feeding the metabolites in the absence of gut bacteria exacerbates motor deficits and neuroinflammation (Sampson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sampson et al., 2016.

claim: Two independent studies found that sodium butyrate treatment alleviates motor deficits and reduces microglial reactivity in MPTP mice with a laboratory microbiota.
source: In contrast, two independent studies found that sodium butyrate treatment alleviates motor deficits and reduces microglial reactivity in 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP) mice with a laboratory microbiota (Hou et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hou et al., 2021 and Liu et al., 2017b.

claim: The findings underscore the need to consider context (GF vs. SPF), diet, and form and duration of intervention in future diet studies in mouse models.
source: Our findings underscore the need to consider context (GF vs. SPF), diet, and form and duration of intervention in future diet studies in mouse models.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the complex and context-dependent effects of SCFAs observed in different studies.

claim: Depletion of microglia using CSF1R inhibitors confers deleterious effects in certain mouse models of PD (MPTP, human α-Syn AAV), LPS-induced sickness behavior, and prion disease.
source: Depletion of microglia using CSF1R inhibitors confers deleterious effects in certain mouse models of PD (MPTP, human α-Syn AAV) (George et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2018), LPS-induced sickness behavior (Vichaya et al., 2020), and prion disease (Carroll et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to George et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2018; Vichaya et al., 2020; and Carroll et al., 2018.

claim: Microglia depletion improves disease outcome in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) and in the 3xTg and 5xFAD mouse models of AD.
source: In contrast, microglia depletion improves disease outcome in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), a preclinical model of multiple sclerosis (Nissen et al., 2018), and in the 3xTg and 5xFAD mouse models of AD (Casali et al., 2020; Spangenberg et al., 2016; Spangenberg et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nissen et al., 2018; Casali et al., 2020; Spangenberg et al., 2016; and Spangenberg et al., 2019.

claim: Depletion of microglia neither exacerbates nor improves motor performance in naïve (control diet) ASO mice.
source: Herein, we found that depletion of microglia neither exacerbates nor improves motor performance in naïve (control diet) mice, suggesting that microglia do not influence behavior in ASO mice, at least in the early stages of disease progression.
evidence: This claim is supported by motor behavior data with PLX5622 treatment shown in Figure 5.

claim: Microglia do not influence behavior in ASO mice, at least in the early stages of disease progression.
source: Herein, we found that depletion of microglia neither exacerbates nor improves motor performance in naïve (control diet) mice, suggesting that microglia do not influence behavior in ASO mice, at least in the early stages of disease progression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PLX5622 motor behavior data in control diet mice.

claim: The protective effects of a prebiotic diet require microglia since their depletion eliminated improvements in motor behavior and αSyn pathology in the brain.
source: In contrast, the protective effects of a prebiotic diet do require microglia since their depletion eliminated improvements in motor behavior and αSyn pathology in the brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by PLX5622 treatment data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The study does not rule out indirect effects of PLX5622 that include reshaping the microbiome to promote motor symptoms in prebiotic diet-fed mice.
source: Our study does not rule out indirect effects of PLX5622 that include reshaping the microbiome to promote motor symptoms in prebiotic diet-fed mice.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of study limitations and alternative interpretations.

claim: Prebiotic intervention significantly increases CSF1 expression in ASO microglia in both the SN and STR.
source: Moreover, we found that prebiotic intervention significantly increases CSF1 expression in ASO microglia in both the SN and STR, potentially implicating CSF1 signaling pathways in mediating the protective effects of prebiotics.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data.

claim: CSF1 signaling pathways may be implicated in mediating the protective effects of prebiotics.
source: Moreover, we found that prebiotic intervention significantly increases CSF1 expression in ASO microglia in both the SN and STR, potentially implicating CSF1 signaling pathways in mediating the protective effects of prebiotics.
evidence: This is speculation based on the CSF1 expression data.

claim: Microglia present a distinct transcriptomic profile and respond to various environmental factors, including the microbiome, in a sex-specific manner.
source: Microglia have been shown to present a distinct transcriptomic profile and respond to various environmental factors, including the microbiome, in a sex-specific manner (Thion et al., 2018; Villa et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Thion et al., 2018 and Villa et al., 2018.

claim: This study probed the effects of prebiotics on microglia in male mice.
source: While this study probed the effects of prebiotics on microglia in male mice, additional insight may come from similar investigation of female animals.
evidence: This describes the scope of the current study.

claim: Prebiotics present a potentially promising therapeutic approach as diet is a significant contributor to microbiome composition.
source: Prebiotics present a potentially promising therapeutic approach as diet is a significant contributor to microbiome composition and epidemiological evidence has linked high-fiber diets with reduced risk of developing PD (Boulos et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the study findings and a citation to Boulos et al., 2019.

claim: Epidemiological evidence has linked high-fiber diets with reduced risk of developing PD.
source: Prebiotics present a potentially promising therapeutic approach as diet is a significant contributor to microbiome composition and epidemiological evidence has linked high-fiber diets with reduced risk of developing PD (Boulos et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Boulos et al., 2019.

claim: Increased intake of fruits, vegetables, and adherence to a Mediterranean diet are associated with a lower risk of PD.
source: While increased intake of fruits, vegetables, and adherence to a Mediterranean diet are associated with a lower risk of PD, individuals consuming a low-fiber, highly processed Western diet exhibit an increased risk of PD diagnosis (Alcalay et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2007; Molsberry et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alcalay et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2007; and Molsberry et al., 2020.

claim: Individuals consuming a low-fiber, highly processed Western diet exhibit an increased risk of PD diagnosis.
source: While increased intake of fruits, vegetables, and adherence to a Mediterranean diet are associated with a lower risk of PD, individuals consuming a low-fiber, highly processed Western diet exhibit an increased risk of PD diagnosis (Alcalay et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2007; Molsberry et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alcalay et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2007; and Molsberry et al., 2020.

claim: Several ongoing clinical trials are exploring the beneficial effects of probiotics and prebiotics on PD-related outcomes.
source: Several ongoing clinical trials are exploring the beneficial effects of probiotics and prebiotics on PD-related outcomes.
evidence: This is a statement about current clinical research.

claim: Gut-targeted therapies offer several advantages compared to traditional therapeutic approaches for brain disorders.
source: Gut-targeted therapies offer several advantages compared to traditional therapeutic approaches for brain disorders.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study findings and general knowledge about drug delivery challenges.

claim: Conventional pharmacological treatments may lose efficacy over time, often fail to treat underlying pathophysiology, and may result in undesirable side effects.
source: Conventional pharmacological treatments rely on chemicals which may lose efficacy over time, often fail to treat underlying pathophysiology, and may result in undesirable side effects for the patient.
evidence: This is general knowledge about limitations of conventional drug treatments.

claim: A notable challenge for CNS-targeting drugs is delivery, requiring drugs that can efficiently cross the blood-brain barrier.
source: A notable challenge for CNS-targeting drugs is delivery, requiring drugs that can efficiently cross the blood-brain barrier.
evidence: This is established knowledge about drug delivery challenges for CNS disorders.

claim: Harnessing safe and practical treatment options, including diet or other microbiome-based approaches, may help accelerate symptomatic relief in PD.
source: Harnessing safe and practical treatment options, including diet or other microbiome-based approaches, may help accelerate symptomatic relief in PD.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic applications based on the study findings.
